collection: NERDC JSS 1 Physical and Health Education physical fitness and body conditioning
note: Original classroom practice. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Relate physical fitness to the demands of everyday movement.
questions.prompt: Which observation gives the clearest evidence of physical fitness for an everyday task?
questions.answer: A pupil carries ordinary class materials to a nearby room and can continue the lesson comfortably.
questions.explanation: Fitness relates to what a person can do. A person’s height, clothes or voice alone do not show capacity for this task.
options: A pupil is taller than everyone in the group.
A pupil carries ordinary class materials to a nearby room and can continue the lesson comfortably.
A pupil wears a sports uniform every day.
A pupil speaks loudly at assembly.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an aspect of fitness can support school participation.
questions.prompt: A group spends part of the school day moving books between two rooms. Explain how muscular endurance could help during this activity, and name a sign that the task is becoming tiring.
questions.answer: Muscular endurance helps the pupil repeat manageable carrying actions. Slower movement or needing more frequent rests can indicate increasing tiredness.
questions.explanation: The activity calls for repeated effort over time. The question concerns the demands of this task.

markingGuide.description: Connects muscular endurance to repeated effort.
Applies the idea to moving books.
Names a plausible observable sign of fatigue.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish balance from agility in movement tasks.
questions.prompt: At a sports lesson, task P asks pupils to hold a steady position. Task Q asks them to change direction quickly in response to a cue. Which pairing best identifies the main fitness component in each task?
questions.answer: P tests balance and Q tests agility.
questions.explanation: Balance helps control a steady position. Agility involves changing direction quickly with control.
options: P tests agility and Q tests balance.
P tests flexibility and Q tests muscular strength.
P tests speed and Q tests flexibility.
P tests balance and Q tests agility.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Explain what one observed activity can show about physical fitness.
questions.prompt: A pupil keeps a steady pace on a short route around the school field. A classmate concludes that the pupil must also have excellent flexibility. Explain what the observation supports and why the conclusion about flexibility needs separate evidence.
questions.answer: It shows that the pupil can sustain that pace for the observed route. Flexibility concerns range of movement and was not measured on the route.
questions.explanation: Fitness has several components. Evidence from one activity may only address some of them.

markingGuide.description: Limits the evidence to maintaining pace during the observed route.
Identifies flexibility as involving range of movement.
Explains why a separate observation would be needed.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Identify body conditioning as planned practice to develop physical capacity.
questions.prompt: A teacher plans several lessons of controlled movement practice, choosing activities to develop strength and flexibility. Why does this plan fit body conditioning?
questions.answer: It uses planned physical practice to develop specific abilities over time.
questions.explanation: Conditioning links repeated practice to physical abilities such as strength and flexibility.
options: It uses planned physical practice to develop specific abilities over time.
It uses the same school hall for each lesson.
It records only who attends the lessons.
It requires every pupil to be ranked by speed.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Demonstrate a teacher-approved stretch with controlled movement and spacing.
questions.prompt: In your own marked space, demonstrate one gentle stretch already taught and approved by your teacher. Show how you enter it slowly, stay within a comfortable range and return to the starting position. A seated version is acceptable.
questions.answer: For example, a pupil gently moves into the teacher’s demonstrated position, briefly maintains it without bouncing, then returns slowly.
questions.explanation: The demonstration assesses control and awareness of space. It uses a movement already taught and selected for the pupil.

markingGuide.description: Uses the marked space without crowding others.
Maintains a controlled position within the selected range.
Returns to the starting position smoothly.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Recognise and address obstacles before a conditioning activity.
questions.prompt: A group is about to practise a familiar conditioning movement on mats. One mat has a folded corner and a school bag lies between the mats. Explain how the pupils should respond before beginning and why each change matters.
questions.answer: Pause and ask the teacher to flatten or replace the mat. Move the bag to the agreed storage area so the practice space and paths between mats are clear.
questions.explanation: A level mat and clear space reduce avoidable tripping or interference during practice.

markingGuide.description: Addresses the folded mat and explains the reason.
Clears the bag from the practice area and explains the reason.
